sources: National Geographic (2012), Crocodiles have strongest bite ever measured (Erickson et al., PLOS ONE): all 23 crocodilian species tested; a 17-foot saltwater crocodile bit with about 3,700 pounds (16,460 newtons), the highest bite force ever recorded; https://www.nationalgeographic.com/animals/article/120315-crocodiles-bite-force-erickson-science-plos-one-strongest

Australian Museum, Estuarine Crocodile: largest reliably measured at least 615 cm; larger ones eat water birds, sea turtles and mammals up to water buffalo size, are cannibalistic and scavenge; cross large stretches of open ocean, found on islands up to 96 km from the mainland; relocated crocodiles found their way back; mound nests up to 2.5 m long; cooler nests tend to produce females and warmer nests males; most attacks are on swimmers or people bending down at the water's edge, and people seized in the water have little chance of escape; https://australian.museum/learn/animals/reptiles/estuarine-crocodile/

Campbell et al. (2010), Estuarine crocodiles ride surface currents to facilitate long-distance travel, Journal of Animal Ecology 79:955-964 (University of Queensland): crocodiles start long-distance travel within an hour of the tide changing; a 3.84 m male travelled 590 km in 25 days riding a seasonal current; https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20546063

beats.say: This crocodile has the strongest bite ever measured.
So I shrank myself down, to see that bite up close.
The saltwater crocodile. The biggest one measured was over six meters long.
Its bite hit about thirty-seven hundred pounds of force.
The strongest bite of any animal scientists have ever tested.
Big ones eat water birds, sea turtles, even water buffalo.
It eats buffalo. Right now, I'm basically a crumb.
It's not just a river animal. It swims out into the open ocean.
Scientists tracked one that surfed five hundred ninety kilometers in twenty-five days.
It waits for the tide to turn, and then surfs it.
They've turned up on islands almost a hundred kilometers from the mainland.
Move a problem croc far away, and it often swims right back home.
Mom builds a nest mound out of plants and mud, up to two and a half meters long.
The nest's heat decides if the babies are boys or girls.
Most attacks hit people swimming, or bending down at the water's edge.
Grabbed in the water, there's very little chance of escape.
Would you go fishing at the water's edge here?
It surfs the ocean, finds its way home, and bites harder than anything ever tested.
